title: A letter to a king
hookLine: Nagarjuna's letter of advice to a royal friend

lines: A PHILOSOPHER WITH A ROYAL FRIEND.
cards: The thinker who wrote of emptiness and two truths also had a friend who was a king. To that friend, tradition says, he wrote a letter. Not a treatise for scholars: a letter, in verse, for a busy man with a kingdom to run.
It's known in Sanskrit as the Suhrllekha, the Letter to a Friend, and it survives in Tibetan and Chinese translations. The philosopher of emptiness, writing advice for a Tuesday.

teach.h: HONOR IT LIKE A WOODEN BUDDHA.
teach.b: The letter begins humbly. Just as the wise honor an image of the Buddha even when it's carved from plain wood, it says, so please honor this advice, even if the verses are poor.
The worth is in what it points to, not the polish. Then it doesn't start with emptiness.
It speaks of generosity, of keeping ethical conduct, of patience, of not drinking to excess, and of eating moderately, like taking medicine. Things a king can actually do between meetings.
Next come the eight worldly concerns: gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and disgrace.
The letter asks the king to meet them all evenly, the good four and the hard four alike, since none of them lasts. For a ruler surrounded by flatterers and critics, that's practical advice.

teach.h: A WEEK OF CARRYING THE TEACHING.
teach.b: And it closes a week. The translators of the Pali Text Society, carrying old words into English. Sitting together, apart, on a screen.
A last look back along the Silk Road and beyond. Then Nagarjuna: the middle way, two truths, no difference.
And now the same teacher, setting down plain advice in a friendly letter. The hardest ideas of the week still needed someone to write them kindly, for one person.

how: Nagarjuna's Letter to a Friend is studied in Tibetan Buddhism as practical advice for lay life, and teachers often explain the eight worldly concerns from it to lay students.

games.why: tradition says Nagarjuna wrote his royal friend a letter: generosity, patience, moderation, and meeting the eight worldly concerns evenly.

practice: In your head, or on paper if one is near, write yourself a short letter of advice, opening the way Nagarjuna did: these are plain words, but take them seriously.
Add two or three lines as a friend would, not a judge: one about something you can actually do, one about meeting praise or blame a little more evenly. Then sit quietly with what you wrote.
